parts.problemMd:
The rate of diffusion of four gases, neon (Ne), hydrogen chloride (HCl), ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>), and oxygen (O<sub>2</sub>), is measured in a sealed container.

What is the order of the rate of diffusion of the gases from slowest to fastest?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The rate of diffusion for gases depends on the relative molecular mass for each gas
- The higher the relative molecular mass, the particles diffuse with more difficulty, and the the rate of diffusion is slower
- Use the Periodic Table to calculate the relative molecular mass (*M*<sub>r</sub>) of all the gases (the relative atomic mass in the case of Ne since it is a monoatomic gas)

  - Ne $M_{r}=20$
  - HCl $M_{r}=1\timesH+1\times\mathrm{Cl}$ $M_{r}=1\times1+1\times35.5$ $M_{r}=36.5$
  - NH<sub>3</sub> $M_{r}=3\timesH+1\timesN$ $M_{r}=3\times1+1\times14$ $M_{r}=17$
  - O<sub>2</sub> $M_{r}=2\timesO$ $M_{r}=2\times16$ $M_{r}=32$
- In order of increasing mass,

  - NH<sub>3</sub> → Ne → O<sub>2</sub> → HCl
- The heavier the gas, the slowest the rate

  - Therefore, the order should be inversed to have the gases ordered from slowest to fastest diffusion rate:
  
    - HCl → O<sub>2</sub> → Ne → NH<sub>3</sub>

The displayed formula of ethanoic acid is shown.

![Displayed structural formula of ethanoic acid: left carbon has three C–H bonds and one C–C bond; right carbon has C–C, C=O double bond, and C–O–H.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/2-atoms-elements-and-compounds/2-3-simple-molecules-and-covalent-bonds/assets/001-displayed-structural-formula-of-ethanoic-acid-le.png)

Which row shows the total number of shared electrons and the total number of non-bonding electrons in one molecule of ethanoic acid?

|   | total number of shared electrons | total number of non-bonding electrons |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 14 | 0 |
| **B** | 14 | 8 |
| **C** | 16 | 0 |
| **D** | 16 | 8 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The following diagram will give a better insight of how electrons are distributed in ethanoic acid molecule

![Dot-and-cross diagram of a two-carbon molecule.

Left carbon forms three C–H single bonds and one C–C single bond. In each C–H bond, one dot (from C) and one cross (from H) are shared. The C–C bond contains one dot and one cross.

Right carbon forms one C–C single bond, one C–O single bond to –OH, and one C=O double bond. The C–O single bond contains one dot and one cross. The C=O double bond contains two shared pairs, each made of one dot and one cross.

The oxygen in the –OH group forms one O–H single bond with one dot and one cross shared. Both oxygen atoms show two lone pairs each, drawn as crosses.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/2-atoms-elements-and-compounds/2-3-simple-molecules-and-covalent-bonds/assets/002-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-a-two-carbon-molecule-l.png)

**Shared electrons (bonding electrons)**

- The total number of electrons involved in the covalent bonds
- Each single bond contains 2 shared electrons, and the double bond contains 4 shared electrons

  - 3 × C–H single bonds = 6 electrons
  - 1 × C–C single bond = 2 electrons
  - 1 × C=O double bond = 4 electrons
  - 1 × C–O single bond = 2 electrons
  - 1 × O–H single bond = 2 electrons
  - **Total shared electrons = 16**

**Non-bonding electrons (lone electrons)**

- These are the outer-shell electrons that are not involved in bonding
- Carbon and hydrogen have no non-bonding electrons
- Both oxygen atoms are in Group VI and have 6 outer electrons
- Each oxygen atom uses 2 electrons for bonding, leaving 4 non-bonding electrons (2 lone pairs) per oxygen atom

  - 2 oxygen atoms × 4 non-bonding electrons = **8 non-bonding electrons**.

**A** & **B** are incorrect as this is the result if a student forgets that the C=O double bond shares 4 electrons and counts it as a single bond, therefore, obtaining 14 shared electrons instead of 16

**C **is incorrect as this is the results of not counting the  non-bonding electrons because they are not shown in the displayed formula of ethanoic acid

> **[exam-tip]**
> If you are not sure on how electrons are connected in the outer shell, your best tool is drawing the dot-and-cross diagram to show which of them are shared, and which of them are not.

parts.problemMd:

|---|---|---|
| **A** | the substances relative atomic or molecular mass in grams | 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> atoms, molecules or formula units |
| **B** | the substances atomic number in grams | 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> atoms, molecules or formula units |
| **C** | the substances relative atomic or molecular mass in grams | 12.04 x 10<sup>23</sup> atoms, molecules or formula units |
| **D** | the substances atomic number in grams | 12.04 x 10<sup>23</sup> atoms, molecules or formula units |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- One mole is the amount of a substance that contains** **$6.02\times10^{23}$ particles and is known as **Avogadro's constant.**
- 1 mole of oxygen, which is a diatomic molecule O<sub>2</sub>, contains** **$6.20\times10^{23}$ **molecules** of oxygen but ** **$2 \times ( 6.02 \times 10^{23} )$ **atoms** of oxygen.
- One mole of any element is equal to the **relative atomic mass** of that element in **grams.** 
E.g. Ca has an *A*<sub>r </sub>of 40, so one mole of Ca has a mass of 40g.
- For a molecule, the relative atomic masses are **added** together. E.g. one mole of NaOH has a mass of 23 + 16 + 1 = 40g.

**B** and **D** are incorrect as the mole refers to the **mass number,** not the atomic number.

**C **is incorrect as the value of Avogadro's constant is  $6.02\times10^{23}.$

parts.problemMd:
How many oxygen atoms are there in 10.0 g of magnesium nitrate, Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>?

(The Avogadro constant, L, is 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

**Step 1:** Calculate the relative formula mass (*M*<sub>r</sub>) of Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2 </sub>using the relative atomic masses from the Periodic Table

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 24 + (2×14) + (6×16)

*M*<sub>r</sub> =24 + 28 + 96 = 148

**Step 2:** Calculate the number of moles of Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>

$\mathrm{moles}=\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

$\mathrm{moles}=\frac{10.0g}{148g\mathrm{mol}^{-1}}$

$\mathrm{moles}=0.06757\mathrm{moles}$

**Step 3:** The fundamental unit of an ionic compound is a formula unit, therefore, the next step is calculating the number of formula units in Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>

$\mathrm{fundamental} \mathrm{units}=\mathrm{moles}\times\mathrm{Avogadro} \mathrm{constant}$

$\text{fundamental units} = 0.06757 \text{mol} \times ( 6.02 \times 10^{23} \text{mol} ^{ - } 1 )$

$\mathrm{fundamental} \mathrm{units}=4.0677\times10^{22}\mathrm{formula} \mathrm{units}$

**Step 4: **Calculate the number of oxygen atoms

According to the chemical formula**, one formula unit of Mg(NO**<sub>**3**</sub>**)**<sub>**2 **</sub>**contains 6 oxygen atoms**, therefore:

$\mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{oxygen} \mathrm{atoms}=\mathrm{formula} \mathrm{units}\times6$

$\mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{oxygen} \mathrm{atoms}=4.0677\times10^{22}\times6$

$\mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{oxygen} \mathrm{atoms}=2.44\times10^{23}\mathrm{oxygen} \mathrm{atoms}$

> **[exam-tip]**
> In multiple-choice calculation questions, the wrong options are often based on **common mistakes**. They usually match answers you would get if you **stop too early** or **misuse the formula**.
> 
> Always complete every step carefully and check the formula before choosing your answer!

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- Molten metal bromides consist of positive metal ions and negative bromide ions
- The positive metal ion will be discharged at the cathode (negative electrode) where they will gain electrons to form the metal
- The negative bromide ions will be discharged at the anode (positive electrode) where they will lose electrons to form bromine

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- The negative electrode is the **cathode**.
- In electrolysis, the cathode attracts positively charged ions (**cations**), which in this case are the hydrogen ions (H<sup>+</sup>).
- At the cathode, hydrogen ions **gain electrons** in a **reduction** reaction to form hydrogen gas.
- The half-equation for this process is:

2H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>-</sup> → H<sub>2</sub> (g)

**A** is incorrect as electrons are **added** to hydrogen ions (reduction), not removed (oxidation).

**C** is incorrect as electrons are **removed from** chloride ions at the positive electrode (anode), not added to them.

**D** is incorrect as electrons travel through the **external circuit** (the wires), not through the electrolyte solution. It is the ions that move through the solution.

parts.problemMd:
Four solutions are separately electrolysed.

|---|---|---|

| **2** | aqueous copper(II) sulfate | copper |
| **3** | concentrated hydrochloric acid | carbon |
| **4** | dilute sulfuric acid | carbon |

In which two experiments is a colourless gas evolved at the anode?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- In experiment 1, oxygen gas is formed at the anode and hydrogen gas at the cathode.
- In experiment 2, copper electrodes are used rather than carbon. Copper is a metal and although unreactive it does influence the outcome at each electrode.
- The negative sulfate ions SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> from the copper sulfate and OH<sup>-</sup> ions from the water are attracted to the anode but both are too stable and so remain in solution.
- The copper anode is oxidised in preference and releases Cu<sup>2+</sup> copper ions into solution hence there is no observable product formed at the anode in experiment 2.
- The end result is a transfer of copper ions from the anode to the cathode which is why this method is used to purify copper.
- In experiment 3, chlorine gas is formed at the anode which is a yellow green colour and hydrogen gas is evolved at the cathode.
- In experiment 4 oxygen gas is formed at the anode and hydrogen gas at the cathode.

A colourless gas is formed at the anode in experiment 1 and 4 only so B is correct.

You might think that since the cathode is the negative electrode then the electrons would not move towards it as like charges repel. The cathode is the negative electrode because it is where reduction takes place (electrons are gained). When it comes to direction of electron flow in electrolysis, remember that they flow in alphabetical order: from the **A**node to the **C**athode.

An iron tray is electroplated with pure silver to improve its appearance. The diagram shows the electrochemical cell with labels X, Y and Z.

![Simple diagram of an electrochemical cell with two electrodes, labelled X and Y, immersed in solution Z, connected to a battery with positive and negative terminals.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/4-electrochemistry/4-2-applications-of-electrolysis/assets/001-simple-diagram-of-an-electrochemical-cell-with-t.png)

Which row correctly identifies the half-equations occurring at electrodes X and Y, and the identity of electrolyte Z?

|   | half-equation at X | half-equation at Y | electrolyte Z |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | Ag<sup>+ </sup>+ e<sup>− </sup>→ Ag | Ag → Ag<sup>+</sup>+ e<sup>−</sup> | aqueous silver nitrate |
| **B** | Ag → Ag<sup>+</sup>+ e<sup>−</sup> | Ag<sup>+ </sup>+ e<sup>− </sup>→ Ag | aqueous silver nitrate |
| **C** | Ag<sup>+ </sup>+ e<sup>− </sup>→ Ag | Fe<sup>2+ </sup>+ 2e<sup>− </sup>→ Fe | aqueous iron(II) nitrate |
| **D** | Fe<sup>2+ </sup>+ 2e<sup>− </sup>→ Fe | Ag → Ag<sup>+</sup>+ e<sup>−</sup> | aqueous silver nitrate |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- **Electrolyte Z:**

  - For electroplating, the electrolyte must be a soluble salt of the metal being plated onto the object
  - Since the tray is being plated with silver, the electrolyte must contain silver ions (Ag<sup>+</sup>)
  - Aqueous silver nitrate is a soluble silver salt.
- **At electrode X (negative electrode / cathode):**

  - The object to be plated (the iron tray) must always be placed at the cathode
  - Here, positive silver ions from the electrolyte are attracted to the negative electrode
  - They are reduced at the electrode where they gain electrons and deposit as solid silver
  - The half-equation is:
  
    - Ag<sup>+ </sup>+ e<sup>− </sup>→ Ag (Reduction)
- **At electrode Y (positive electrode / anode):**

  - The pure plating metal (silver) must be placed at the anode
  - The silver atoms lose electrons (oxidized) to continually replace the silver ions in the electrolyte
  - The half-equation is:
  
    - Ag → Ag<sup>+</sup>+ e<sup>−</sup> (Oxidation).

**B **is incorrect as the half equations are swapped

**C **is incorrect as uses iron(II) nitrate as the electrolyte

**D** is incorrect as at X (cathode), silver ions should be reduced to form a silver coating, not  iron ions. The half-equation Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Fe would deposit iron, not silver.

> **[exam-tip]**
> In electroplating questions, examiners often use a **3-column table** to test whether you understand the entire setup, not just half-equations.
> 
> A common trap is choosing an option that has correct half-equations but places the **object to be plated at the anode**.
> 
> Remember the fundamental rule: the object being coated must always be the **cathode (negative electrode)**.

There is an **increase in temperature **in **exothermic **reactions, while there is a **decrease in temperature **in **endothermic **reactions

- Work out the change in temperature for each reaction $c h a n g e i n t e m p e r a t u r e ( \Delta T ) = f i n a l t e m p e r a t u r e - i n i t i a l t e m p e r a t u r e$

parts.problemMd:
Chlorine and ethane react together in an exothermic reaction to produce chloroethane and hydrogen chloride. The equation for the reaction is shown below.

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl + HCl

The table below shows the relevant bond energies.

| **bond** | **bond energy / (kJ / mol)** |
|---|---|
| CーCl | + 340 |
| CーC | + 350 |
| CーH | + 410 |
| ClーCl | + 240 |
| HーCl | + 430 |

What is the energy change for the reaction between chlorine and ethane?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** A**** because:**

- The reaction is exothermic hence the energy change must be **negative**.
- Bonds broken:

  - One C-H bond in ethane (410 kJ / mol)
  - One Cl-Cl in chlorine (240 kJ / mol)
- Total energy required to break bonds:

  - 410 + 240 = 650 kJ / mol.
- Bonds formed:

  - One C-Cl bond in chloroethane (340 kJ / mol)
  - One H-Cl in hydrogen chloride (430 kJ / mol)
- Total energy released during bond formation:

  - 340 + 430 = 770 kJ / mol.
- *ΔH* = energy needed to break bonds - energy given out when bonds form.
- ΔH = 650 - 770 = -120 kJ / mol.

**B**,** C **and **D** are incorrect as these options do not produce the correct result.

|---|---|

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** C**** because:**

- Energy required to break bonds: 945 + (3 x 436) = 2253 kJ / mol.
- Energy released during bond formation: 6 x 390 = 2340 kJ / mol.

parts.problemMd:

| **bond** | **bond energy / (kJ / mol)** |
|---|---|
| HーCl | +430 |
| HーH | +436 |
| ClーCl | - |

What is the energy of the Cl─Cl bond?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** B**** because:**

- *ΔH* = energy needed to break bonds - energy given out when bonds form.
- Substitute the values into the equation and let *X* be the energy of the Cl─Cl bond:
- -184 = (436 + *X*) - (2 x 430) kJ / mol.
- Rearrange and solve for *X *:
- *X* = (-184) + (2 x 430) - (436) = +240 kJ / mol

**A**,** C **and **D** are incorrect as these options do not produce the correct result.

parts.problemMd:

CH<sub>4</sub> + 2O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O

| **bond** | **bond energy / (kJ / mol)** |
|---|---|
| HーO | +460 |
| O＝O | +496 |
| CーH | +410 |
| C＝O | - |

What is the energy of the C＝O bond?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** D**** because:**

- Calculate the energy needed to break bonds:

bonds broken** = **4 x C-H and 2 x O=O

bonds broken** = **(4 x 410) + (2 x 496)

bonds broken** = **2632

- Calculate the energy given out when bonds form:

bonds formed = 2X + (4 x O-H)

bonds formed = 2X + (4 x 460)

bonds formed = 2X + 1840

- *ΔH* = energy needed to break bonds - energy given out when bonds form.

- Substitute the values into the equation and let *X* be the energy of the C＝O bond:

*ΔH* = bonds broken - bonds formed

-890 = 2632 - [2*X* + 1840]

-890 = 2632 - 2*X *- 1840

-890 = (2632 - 1840) - 2*X*

- Rearrange and solve for *X*:

2*X* = 792 + 890

2*X = *1682

*X* = +841 kJ / mol

**A**,** B** and **C** are incorrect as these options do not produce the correct result.

parts.problemMd:
Reversible reactions occur when products formed in the forward reaction behave as reactants and proceed in the reverse direction to produce the original reactants again.

| **3** | Both directions are exothermic |
| **4** | Both directions are endothermic |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** A**** **

- The energetics of reversible reactions are such that if the forward direction is exothermic, then the reverse direction is the **opposite**, hence endothermic.
- This applies in both cases, so if the forward reaction is endothermic, then the reverse reaction must be exothermic.

**B** and **D** are incorrect as both directions will not have the same energy change.

**C** is incorrect as statements 1 and 2 are both true.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:

- From the balanced equation there are **4 moles** of gaseous reactants to **2 moles** of gaseous product.
- An increase in pressure would shift the equilibrium to the side with **less** gaseous moles, favouring the **forward reaction.**
- Therefore the percentage yield of ammonia **increases.**

**A** is incorrect as the percentage yield increases with increasing pressure.

**C** and **D** are incorrect as the rate if production increases with increasing pressure.

parts.problemMd:

- An increase in pressure would shift the equilibrium to the side with **less** **volume**, so it would favour the forward reaction and **increase** the yield of methanol.

**A**, **B** and **D** are incorrect as these conditions would not provide the highest yield of methanol.

parts.problemMd: What is the oxidation state of Fe in Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** D**** **

- Oxidation number refers to a single** atom** or **ion** which can be on their own or in a compound.
- The oxidation number of a compound is **0** and of an element is also **0**.
- The oxidation number of an ion is equal to the **charge** of that ion e.g. F<sup>ー</sup> is  -1.
- The oxidation number of **oxygen** in a compound is always **-2** (except in peroxide R-O-O-R, where it is **-1**).
- There are 3 oxygens in Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>,  so 3 x -2 = -6.
- As it is a compound, the overall charge must be 0, hence each Fe atom must be +3 since 2 x 3 = 6  and +6 - 6 = 0.

**A**, **B** and **C** are incorrect as these options do not provide an oxidation number of 0 for the compound.

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** D**** **

- For FeCl<sub>3</sub> it's (III) as the oxidation state of Fe is **+3** as each Cl is -1.

**A**,** B** and **C** are incorrect as these names do not correctly match with the formulae.

parts.problemMd:
Aqueous copper(II) sulfate reacts with zinc according to the equation shown.

Zn (s) + CuSO<sub>4</sub>(aq) → ZnSO<sub>4</sub>(aq) + Cu(s)

Which row correctly identifies the oxidising agent and the reducing agent in this reaction?

|   | oxidising agent | reducing agent |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | CuSO<sub>4</sub> | Zn |
| **B** | Zn | CuSO<sub>4</sub> |
| **C** | Cu | ZnSO<sub>4</sub> |
| **D** | ZnSO<sub>4</sub> | Cu |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

To identify the agents (**which are always at the reactants**), you must first determine what is being oxidised and what is being reduced by looking at the electron transfer or changes in oxidation number

- **Zinc (Zn) **

  - The zinc atom goes from an oxidation state of 0 in Zn(s) to +2 in  ZnSO<sub>4 </sub>(aq)
  - The oxidation number of Zn has increased, this implies that Zn has lost electrons (oxidised)
  - Since zinc is **oxidised**, the substance that is oxidised acts as the **reducing agent** because it gives electrons to the other substance forcing it to reduce
- **Copper(II) sulfate (CuSO**<sub>**4**</sub>**) **

  - The copper ion goes from an oxidation state of +2 in CuSO<sub>4 </sub>(aq) to 0 in solid Cu(s)
  - The oxidation number of Cu has decreased this implies that Cu has gained electrons (reduced)
  - Since copper is** reduced**, the substance that is reduced acts as the **oxidising agent** because it takes electrons from the other substance forcing it to oxidise

**B** is incorrect as the agents are swapped

**C** & **D **are incorrect as oxidising and reducing agents must always be in the *reactants*

**Step 3: **Solve

+1 + Mn − 8 = 0
Mn = +7

parts.problemMd:
Propanoic acid is a weak acid.

What is a possible pH for a dilute aqueous solution of propanoic acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The pH scale is used to measure the acidity or alkalinity of a solution
- Acids have a pH of less than 7
- Propanoic acid is a **weak acid**

  - Weak acids partially dissociates into their ions in aqueous solution

- Since pH depends on the concentration of hydrogen ions (H<sup>+</sup>), a weak acid produces fewer H<sup>+</sup> ions than a strong acid when they are mixed with water, so its pH is below 7 but not very low
- Therefore, its pH will be closer to neutral, typically between pH 4 and pH 6

Element **X **is found in Group 7 of the Periodic Table.

Which properties are typical of element **X**?

| **1** | Poor conductor of electricity |
|---|---|
| **2** | Malleable |
| **3** | High melting points |
| **4** | Form acidic oxides |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** **

- Elements in Group 7 are non- metals
- Non metals are poor conductors of electricity due to the lack of charged particles that can move freely
- Non- metals can also form acidic oxides

**A**, **C **and **D **are incorrect as Group 7 elements typically have low melting points due to weak intermolecular forces between molecules and are not malleable

parts.problemMd:
The table shows the densities at room temperature of halogens W, X, Y and Z

| halogens | density at room temperature / g/cm<sup>3</sup> |
|---|---|
| W | 0.0017 |
| X | 3.1 |
| Y | 0.0032 |
| Z | 4.93 |

Which row correctly identifies W, X, Y and Z?

|   | W | X | Y | Z |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | fluorine | chlorine | bromine | iodine |
| **B** | fluorine | bromine | chlorine | iodine |
| **C** | iodine | chlorine | bromine | fluorine |
| **D** | iodine | bromine | chlorine | fluorine |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Density of halogens increases down Group VII  because atoms get larger and intermolecular forces get stronger, therefore, the halogens become denser as you go down the group
- At room temperature, fluorine and chlorine are gases, so they will have very low density

  - **W** has the lowest density of the table, 0.0017 g/cm<sup>3</sup> , so** W is fluorine**
  - **Y** has the next lowest density of the table, 0.0032 g/cm<sup>3</sup> , so** Y is chlorine**
- Bromine is a liquid at room temperature, so it must have a higher density than fluorine and chlorine

  - **X **has a density of 3.1 g/cm<sup>3  </sup>which matches **bromine**
- Iodine is a solid at room temperature and is the densest halogen listed. **Z **has the highest density (4.93 g/cm<sup>3</sup>) , so its **iodine**

parts.problemMd:
Lithium and chromium are metals.

Which statement about the properties of these elements is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Chromium is a transition metal
- Transition metals can have more than one oxidation state (e.g. Cr<sup>2+</sup>, Cr<sup>3+</sup>).
- **Different oxidation states** give rise to **coloured compounds**, which is a key property of transition metals

**A **is incorrect because lithium reacts with water, but chromium does not react vigorously with water, therefore the statement is false

**B **is incorrect because although both are metals which particles are arranged in a metallic lattice, **the melting point of transition metals is significantly higher than Group I metals**. Therefore, lithium and chromium have very different melting points

**C **is incorrect because  lithium is a **Group I metal** and **only forms 1+ ions**, so it does not have multiple oxidation states and does not form coloured compounds

parts.problemMd:
The early Periodic table was used to classify the known elements and was used to predict the properties of the elements that had not yet been discovered.

Which row correctly describes how this was possible?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** B**** **

- There are **patterns** in the way the elements are arranged on the Periodic table, there are also patterns and trends in the **chemical** **behaviour** of the elements.
- In this way the Periodic table can be used to predict how an unknown element will behave and was used to **identify** them.

**A** is incorrect as elements in the same Period tend to behave **differently**.

**C **is incorrect as elements in different Groups have **different** **properties** as they have different outer shell **electron** **configurations**. Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell and share similar properties.

**D **is incorrect as the elements were positioned according to their **atomic** **number** and **chemical** properties.

parts.problemMd:
Potassium and krypton are elements in Period 4. Potassium is at the beginning of the period and is more metallic than krypton which is at the end of the period.

What makes potassium more metallic than krypton?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** D**** **

- The change in metallic to non-metallic character as we move across the Periodic table from left to right is linked to the **electronic configuration** of the elements.
- Non-metals have **more electrons** in their outer shells than metals.
- Potassium is in **Group I **and has **1** electron in its outer shell whereas krypton is in **Group VIII** and has **8** electrons in its outer shell.

**A** and **B** are incorrect as although potassium has fewer electrons and protons than krypton, it is the **outer shell electrons** that determine its chemical properties.

**C **is incorrect as both elements are in the same period they have the same number of electron shells.

parts.problemMd:
The elements of the Periodic table can be broadly classified into two main characters which are metals and nonmetals. Which statements are correct?

| **1** | Magnesium is more metallic than silicon. |
|---|---|
| **2** | Boron is more metallic than lithium. |
| **3** | Carbon is less metallic than beryllium. |
| **4** | Sodium is less metallic than aluminium. |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** A**** **

- Magnesium lies further to the **left** than silicon, hence it has a greater metallic character than silicon.
- Beryllium is further **left** than carbon, hence it also has greater metallic character than carbon.

**B**,** C** and **D** are incorrect as as lithium and sodium are both more metallic than boron and aluminium as they lie further on the left of the Periodic table.

parts.problemMd:
The metallic character of the elements changes as you move across a period.

Which statement explains this trend?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** C**** **

- Metallic character of elements **decreases** as you move across a period and is linked to the number of outer shell electrons in each element.
- Elements on the right more **readily accept electrons** to fill their valence shells as it is easier for them to gain a small number of electrons than it is to lose a large number of them.
- Elements on the left are more likely to **lose** outer electrons, exposing a full  valence shell ‘below’.

**A**,** B** and **D** are incorrect as although these statements are correct they do not explain the trend in metallic character.

parts.problemMd:
An element has an electronic configuration of 2,8,6.

Which group and period can the element be found in?

|   | **group** | **period** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 6 | 3 |
| **B** | 6 | 8 |
| **C** | 3 | 6 |
| **D** | 8 | 2 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** **

- The electronic configuration shows the arrangement of electrons in their shells
- The last notation is the number of electrons in the outer shell
- The number of electrons in the outer shell correlates to the group number

  - 2,8,**6 **shows there are six electrons in the outer shell so the element is in Group 6
- The period number refers to the number of shells an atom has
- The number of notations shows the number of shells

  - 2,8,6 has three notations so the element has three shells and is in Period 3

**B**, **C** and **D** are incorrect as the group or period number is wrong

Why is potassium placed after argon?

- The elements are arranged on the Periodic Table in order of increasing atomic  number.
- Argon has 22 neutrons while potassium has 20 but argon has **18 protons **while  potassium has **19**.
- Argon has therefore the higher relative atomic mass of the two elements but is listed before potassium as it has a **smaller** **atomic** **number**.

**B **is incorrect as potassium has a **higher** atomic number than argon (and therefore less protons).

parts.problemMd:
**X**, **Y** and **Z** are the halogens chlorine, bromine and iodine, but not necessarily in that order.

When aqueous **Y** is added to an aqueous solution containing ions of **Z**, a brown solution is formed. When aqueous **X** is added to an aqueous solution containing ions of **Z**, no reaction occurs

Which row correctly identifies halogens X, Y and Z?

|   | X | Y | Z |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | bromine | chlorine | iodine |
| **B** | iodine | chlorine | bromine |
| **C** | iodine | bromine | chlorine |
| **D** | chlorine | iodine | bromine |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Halogens are Group VII non-metals
- In terms of reactivity, a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide ion from its aqueous solution
- The reactivity decreases down the group (chlorine > bromine > iodine)
- When a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen in aqueous state, the less reactive halogen will be observed in the mixture

  - It is important to recap the  appearance of the halogens
  
    - Chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas, bromine is a red-brown liquid, and iodine is a grey-black solid (brown in solution)
- A brown solution is formed when aqueous Y is added to ions of Z

  - A brown solution in water can indicate that bromine (red-brown liquid) or iodine (typically grey solid, but brown in aqueous) was formed
  - This means that** Z is less reactive than Y**

- When aqueous X is added to Z ions, **no reaction occurs**

  - This means **X is less reactive than Z**
  - In consequence, **X is** **less reactive than Y**

- Therefore, in order of decreasing reactivity:

  - Y >  Z  >  X

- Since, reactivity decreases down the group (chlorine > bromine > iodine)

  - Y = chlorine, Z = bromine, X = iodine

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** C**** **

- Rubidium is a **Group I **metal which loses its **single outer shell electron**, forming positively charged ions, Rb<sup>+</sup>.
- Bromine is a **Group VII** halogen which requires just **one electron** to complete its outer  shell, forming the negatively charged ion Br<sup>-</sup>.
- Both ions attract in a 1:1 ratio forming the ionic compound **RbBr**.
- The salts of the metals in Group I, II and III are generally **white solids**, hence RbBr is white.

**A** and **B **are incorrect as the compound formed is a white solid.

**D **is incorrect as the formula for rubidium bromide is RbBr.

|---|---|---|
| **A** | `✓` | `✓` |
| **B** | `✓` | $\times$ |
| **C** | $\times$ | `✓` |
| **D** | $\times$ | $\times$ |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** B**** **

- Element Q has displaced bromine from the compound KBr, so it must therefore be more reactive than bromine as reactivity **decreases** moving down Group VII.
- The atomic mass also **increases** moving down the group as subatomic particles are added on.
- Element Q is thus **more** **reactive** than bromine and has a **lower** relative atomic mass.

**A **is incorrect as since Q is more reactive than bromine it must sit above it so its relative atomic mass must be **less** than that of bromine.

**C **and** D** are incorrect as Q is more reactive than bromine since it **displaced bromine** from KBr.

parts.problemMd:

What is present in the reaction mixture?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** C**

- In Group VII reactivity decreases moving down the group and the atomic radius increases, so the outer shell gets further from the nucleus.
- The attraction between the nucleus and electrons gets weaker, so an electron is less easily gained, making it more difficult for the halogens to receive electrons.
- For the halogen in solution to displace the halide from the lithium halide, it must sit above the halide
- Chlorine in above iodine in the Periodic Table so chlorine will displace iodine from lithium iodide to produce lithium chloride and iodine

  - chlorine + lithium iodide → lithium chloride + iodine
- Aqueous iodine is a brown solution, so as iodine is produced, the reaction mixture will darken

**A** and **B** are incorrect as bromine sits **below **both chlorine and fluorine and cannot displace them as it is less reactive than both.

**D **is incorrect as chlorine sits** below** fluorine.

parts.problemMd:
Four statements about Group I metals are shown.

1. They share similar physical properties because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell.
2. Reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and is more easily lost.
3. Transition elements have higher melting points than Group I metals because the metallic bonding in Group I metals is weaker.
4. Group I metals form soluble acidic oxides which dissolve in water to form solutions with a high pH.

Which statements are correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- **Statement 1 is incorrect**

  - Elements in the same group share similar **chemical** properties, not physical properties, because of their outer shell electrons
  - Group I metals actually show a trend in physical properties (e.g., melting point decreases down the group).
- **Statement 2 is correct**

  - As you go down Group I, the atoms get larger
  - The single outer electron is further from the positive nucleus, meaning the electrostatic attraction is weaker, making the electron easier to lose
  - Metals like to lose electrons, therefore, if the electron is easier to lose the reactivity is greater

- **Statement 3 is correct**

  - Transition elements are generally much harder and have much higher melting points than Group I metals
  - This is because transition elements have stronger metallic lattices.
- **Statement 4 is incorrect**

  - While Group I oxides do dissolve in water to form high pH (alkaline) solutions, metals form **basic** oxides, not acidic oxides
  - Acidic oxides are formed by non-metals (like sulfur or carbon)

> **[exam-tip]**
> In multiple-choice questions, examiners often combine **one correct idea and one incorrect idea** in the same statement.
> 
> If one part is wrong, the whole statement is wrong, even if another part sounds correct.
> 
> Do not skim for keywords like “high pH.” Read the entire statement carefully before deciding.

parts.problemMd:
A student investigates the reactivity of four different metals by adding a small piece of each metal to separate test-tubes containing aqueous iron(II) chloride.

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

This question is based on the principle that **a more reactive metal will displace another**. Therefore,  according to the reactivity series of metals in decreasing order of reactivity: **magnesium > aluminium > zinc > iron > copper**.

- **Copper**

  - Copper is less reactive than iron, so it cannot displace iron from its aqueous salt. **No reaction (**×**)**
- **Magnesium**

  - Magnesium is more reactive than iron, so a displacement reaction occurs. **Reaction (**✓**)**
- **Zinc**

  - Zinc is more reactive than iron, so a displacement reaction occurs. **Reaction (**✓**)**
- **Aluminium**

  - Aluminium is more reactive than iron, so a displacement reaction occurs. **Reaction (**✓**)**

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** C**** because:**

- **Sacrificial rust protection **works by using a metal placed **higher** up on the reactivity series and connecting it to the object that needs to be protected.
- Zinc is a more reactive metal so is more likely to **lose** **electrons** (and become oxidised) than iron and it readily donates its electrons to any iron ions that might have formed, stopping them from corroding.
- The zinc metal will be **corroded** **in** **preference** to the steel hull, hence preventing it from rusting.

**A**, **B** and **D** are incorrect as the sacrificial metal must be **above iron** on the reactivity series to be able to oxidise before the iron atoms do.

Which statement is correct for the zones X, Y and Z?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- **Zone Z (bottom)**

  - Hot air is blown into the furnace
  - Coke burns in oxygen carbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide
  - This reaction produces a lot of heat and does not reduce the iron ore
  - The purpose of this zone is to generate heat and carbon dioxide
- **Zone Y (middle)**

  - Carbon dioxide rises and reacts with more hot coke carbon dioxide + carbon → carbon monoxide
  - This produces carbon monoxide
  
    - Carbon monoxide is the key reducing agent
    - The reducing agent will remove oxygen from the iron oxide (iron ore) to form pure iron
  - No iron is produced yet
- **Zone X (upper region)**

  - Iron(III) oxide from hematite meets rising carbon monoxide
  - The main reduction reaction happens iron (III) oxide  + carbon monoxide → iron + carbon dioxide
  - Carbon monoxide removes oxygen from iron(III) oxide
  
    - Iron(III) oxide is reduced to iron
    - Carbon monoxide is oxidised to carbon dioxide
- Reduction requires carbon monoxide
- Carbon monoxide reacts with iron(III) oxide in zone X
- Therefore, iron(III) oxide is reduced in X

**A **& **B **are incorrect because carbon dioxide is used up in Y, not produced. Therefore, carbon dioxide is not a product in both Y and Z

**C **is incorrect because the reduction of iron (III) oxide requires carbon monoxide. In Zone Y, carbon monoxide is being formed, not used. Iron(III) oxide is reduced above this zone, where carbon monoxide reacts with the ore. Therefore, iron(III) oxide is not reduced in Y

Iron is produced in a blast furnace.

What are the reasons for blowing in oxygen and adding calcium oxide?

|---|---|---|
| **A** | reacts with carbon so removes it | removes basic impurities making slag |
| **B** | oxygen reacts with iron | reacts with slag and so removes it |
| **C** | oxygen reacts with iron | removes acidic impurities making slag |
| **D** | reacts with carbon so removes it | removes acidic impurities making slag |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D ****because:**

- When oxygen is blown into the furnace it reacts with carbon to form carbon dioxide
- The carbon dioxide reacts with more carbon forming carbon monoxide which can reduce iron(III) oxide to iron
- Calcium oxide is formed from the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate (which is added to remove impurities in the ore)
- The calcium oxide will react with acidic impurities such as silicon dioxide to form calcium silicate, or slag which can be removed

**A **is incorrect as calcium oxide will not react with basic impurities as it is a basic oxide itself

**B** is incorrect as oxygen reacts with carbon, not iron, and slag is formed as a result of calcium oxide reacting with acidic impurities

**C** is incorrect as oxygen reacts with carbon not iron

Which row shows the correct balanced equations for the main reactions occurring in zones X, Y and Z?

|   | zone X | zone Y | zone Z |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | C + O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> | C + CO<sub>2</sub>→ 2CO | Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO<sub>2</sub> |
| **B** | C + O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> | CaCO<sub>3</sub>→ CaO+CO<sub>2</sub> | Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO<sub>2</sub> |
| **C** | Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO<sub>2</sub> | C + O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> | C + CO<sub>2</sub>→ 2CO |
| **D** | Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO<sub>2</sub> | C + CO<sub>2</sub>→ 2CO | C + O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

The flow of gases rise from the bottom of the furnace to the top

- **Zone Z (bottom)**

  - Hot air (oxygen) is blasted into the bottom of the furnace, where it reacts with the carbon (coke) in a highly exothermic reaction to provide the heat for the furnace
  - The highly exothermic combustion provides the heat needed for the furnace
  - The CO<sub>2</sub> produced then rises to react with more coke
  
    - The equation is: C + O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub>

  - As the carbon dioxide rises, it reacts with more carbon (coke) to form carbon monoxide.
  
    - The equation is: C + CO<sub>2</sub>→ 2CO
- **Zone X (top)**

  - The carbon monoxide continues to rise to the top of the furnace, where it acts as the reducing agent, reducing the descending iron(III) oxide (hematite) to form iron.
  
    - The equation is: Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO<sub>2</sub>

**A **& **B **are incorrect as zone X is where the reduction of iron (III) oxide occurs, not the formation of carbon dioxide

**C **is incorrect as the zone Z  is where the carbon dioxide is produced

parts.problemMd:
Water from a reservoir contains insoluble solids and harmful microbes. The water must be treated to make it safe for the domestic water supply.

Which row shows the correct order of the stages used to treat the water?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Water from reservoir can contain big insoluble particles, big insoluble particles and microbes
- Filtration of big insoluble particles is done first to remove large solids such as leaves or rocks

  - This will prevent damaging or blockage in later stages of the treatment
- Sedimentation allows smaller suspended solids to settle under gravity because they are denser than water

  - This is done before the filtration of small particles to make the filtration of small particles more effective
  - If the fine filtration were done first, the filter can block quickly, reducing the efficiency
- Once the particles settle down by the action of gravity, filtration of small insoluble particles is performed

  - This removes remaining fine particles that did not settle in the sedimentation
- Chlorination is carried out last to kill harmful microorganisms

  - Doing this earlier would be ineffective because particles can protect microbes from chlorine
- Therefore, the correct order is **filtration of big insoluble particles → sedimentation → filtration of small insoluble particles →  chlorination**

**A **is incorrect because sedimentation is placed after filtration of small particles, but particles must settle before fine filtration is effective

**B **is incorrect because chlorination is carried out before final filtration, which can remove chlorine and reduce disinfection effectiveness

**D** is incorrect because chlorination is done too early and insoluble solids would reduce its ability to kill microbes

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Fertilisers must supply nutrients in a soluble, plant-available form
- Plants absorb potassium as K⁺ and nitrogen as NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> or NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>
- Evaluate each compound:

  - Ca<sub>3</sub>N<sub>2</sub><sup>  </sup>: Contains nitrogen, but as a nitride
  
    - Not a suitable fertiliser because of the presence of nitride and calcium ions
  - K<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> : Contains potassium (K⁺)
  
    - Suitable source of soluble potassium
  - Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>: Contains no potassium and no nitrogen usable by plants
  
    - Even if phosphate is source of phosphorus, which is a suitable NPK fertiliser, calcium is not
    - Calcium salts are usually insoluble in water which make this compound not feasible
  - NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>: Contains ammonium and nitrate, both usable nitrogen sources
  
    - It supplies a high amount of nitrogen
- The best combination that supplies potassium and nitrogen is 2 and 4

**A**, **C **& **D **are incorrect because they do not supply nitrogen or potassium as K⁺, NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> or NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

Different fertilisers contain the essential elements needed for plant growth in varying quantities.

Which fertiliser compound contains the highest percentage by mass of the essential elements needed for growth?

[Relative atomic masses, *A*<sub>r</sub>: H = 1; N = 14; O = 16; P = 31; S = 32; K = 39; Ca = 40]
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- It has a percentage by mass of 44.8% which is more than the other fertiliser compounds
- To answer this question, you need to determine the percentage by mass of the essential elements for all of the fertilisers
- **Remember**: The essential elements are nitrogen, phosphorous and potassium (NPK)
- To calculate the percentage by mass, use the following equation:

  - % by mass = $\frac{\mathrm{total} \mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{the} \mathrm{element} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{the} \mathrm{compound}}{M_{r}\mathrm{of} \mathrm{the} \mathrm{compound}}\times100$
- For (**N**H<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>

  - % by mass = $\frac{2 \times 14}{2 \times ( 14 + ( 4 \times 1 ) ) + 32 + ( 4 \times 16 ) } \times 100$= 21.2%
- For **N**H<sub>4</sub>**N**O<sub>3</sub>

  - % by mass =  $\frac{2\times14}{(2\times14)+(4\times1)+(3\times16)}\times100$= 35.0%
- For **K**<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>

  - % by mass = $\frac{2\times39}{(2\times39)+32+(4\times16)}\times100$= 44.8%
- Ca<sub>3</sub>(**P**O<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>

  - % by mass =  $\frac{2 \times 31}{ \text{stretchy} ( 3 \times 40 \text{stretchy} ) + 2 \times ( 31 + \text{stretchy} ( 4 \times 16 ) \text{stretchy} )} \times 100$= 20%

|---|---|---|---|

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction in which carbon dioxide and water react to form glucose and oxygen

What is the maximum mass of glucose that can be produced from 40 cm<sup>3</sup> of carbon dioxide?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A ****because:**

- The number of moles of carbon dioxide gas = volume (cm<sup>3</sup>) ÷ 24000 = 40 ÷ 24000 = 1.67 x 10<sup>-3</sup> moles
- You need to use the balanced symbol equation to work out how many moles of glucose this will produce - this is an equation that you are expected to know:

  - 6CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6O<sub>2</sub>
- For every 1 mole of carbon dioxide, there will be 6 times less glucose:

  - Number of moles of glucose = 1.67 x 10<sup>-3</sup> ÷ 6 = 2.78 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol
- Mass of glucose = moles x *M*<sub>r</sub>
- To calculate *M*<sub>r </sub>of glucose: (6 x 12) + (12 x 1) + (6 x 16) = 180
- Therefore, mass = 2.78 x 10<sup>-4 </sup>x 180 = 0.05 g

**B** is incorrect as the moles of carbon dioxide has not been divided by 6

**C** is incorrect as the volume of gas was divided by 24

**D** is incorrect as the volume of gas was divided by 24 and the moles of CO<sub>2 </sub>hasn't been divided by 6

- Two carbons

  - 2*n *+ 2 = 6
  - The alkane formula would be C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>
- Four carbons

  - *n* = 4
  - If this was an alkane, then 2*n *+ 2 = 10
  - The alkane formula would be C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>
  - This matches **C**
- Five carbons

  - *n* = 5
  - If this was an alkane, then 2*n *+ 2 = 12
  - The alkane formula would be C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>

**A **is incorrect as this is **ethene,** an alkene.

**B **is incorrect as this is **butene,** an alkene.

**D **is incorrect as this is **pentene,** an alkene.

parts.problemMd:
Petroleum is separated into fractions by fractional distillation.

Which statement about the properties of the fractions is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Crude oil (petroleum) is a mixture of hydrocarbons with different chain lengths
- In **fractional distillation**, crude oil is heated so that most of it vaporises
- The vapours enter a **fractionating column**, which is **hot at the bottom and cooler at the top**

  - Hydrocarbons with **high boiling points** (long-chain molecules) **condense low down** in the column
  - Hydrocarbons with **low boiling points** (short-chain molecules) **rise higher** before condensing
- As chain length increases, hydrocarbons have **stronger intermolecular forces**

  - Stronger intermolecular forces mean **higher boiling points**, **higher viscosity**, and **lower volatility**
  - This explains why fractions with longer carbon chains are more viscous liquids
- Therefore, the viscosity of the fractions increases as chain length increases, so C is correct

**A **is incorrect because fractions with more carbon atoms have higher boiling points, not lower. This is because larger molecules have strong intermolecular forces of attraction

**B **is incorrect because fractions with small molecules have low boiling points and rise to the top of the fractionating column

**D **is incorrect because refinery gases contain short-chain hydrocarbons, which are more volatile than long-chain hydrocarbons

parts.problemMd:
X, Y and Z are organic compounds.

Some properties of these compounds are listed.

- Y and Z decolourise bromine water, while X does not.
- X and Z has the same number of carbons. Y has one carbon atom more in the chain.
- X is manufactured by the hydration of Z with steam.

Which row identifies correctly X, Y and Z?

|   | X | Y | Z |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | ethanol | propene | ethene |
| **B** | ethanol | butene | ethene |
| **C** | ethene | propene | ethanol |
| **D** | ethene | butene | ethanol |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The bromine water test is used to distinguish between alkenes and other organic compounds
- Substances that decolourise bromine water are unsaturated hydrocarbons (alkenes)
- This is because the bromine diatomic (Br<sub>2</sub>) can react via an **addition reaction **across C=C double bond, turning the orange bromine water into colourless

  - Since Y and Z can decoulourise bromine water, Y and Z must be alkenes
  - X does not decolourise bromine water, so X is not an alkene
- X and Z have the same number of carbon atoms
- Y has one more carbon atom than X and Z

  - By checking the rows of the table, if Z is ethene (2 carbons), then Y must be propene (3 carbons)
  - If Z is ethene then X must start with the prefix **eth-**
- X is manufactured by the hydration of Z with steam
- Hydration is the process of adding water (steam) to the C=C double bond
- One hydrogen of water will bond to one carbon, while the OH group will bond to the other carbon

  - The hydration of ethene produces ethanol
  - Therefore Z = ethene and X = ethanol
- Putting it all together:

  - X = ethanol
  - Y = propene
  - Z = ethene

**B **& **D **is incorrect because Y is not butene. Butene has two more carbons than ethene, not one

**C **is incorrect Z is not ethanol. Ethanol is not an unsaturated hydrocarbon and it does not decolourise bromine water

parts.problemMd:
Ethanol can be manufactured by fermentation or by the catalytic addition of steam to ethene

Three statements comparing these two processes are shown.

1. The hydration of ethene uses non-renewable raw materials, whereas fermentation uses renewable raw materials.
2. Hydration is carried out as a batch process, making it less efficient than fermentation.
3. Hydration requires high temperatures and pressures, whereas fermentation requires a low and controlled temperature.

Which statements are correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- **Statement 1 is correct**

  - The ethene used in hydration is obtained from the cracking of fractions of petroleum (crude oil), which is a finite, **non-renewable** resource
  - Fermentation uses glucose obtained from crops like sugar cane or maize, which are **renewable** raw materials
- **Statement 2 is incorrect**

  - Hydration is a **continuous process**, which is very fast and efficient
  - Fermentation is a **batch process** which is slow and inefficient because the reaction vessel must be emptied and cleaned after every batch
- **Statement 3 is correct**

  - Hydration requires high temperatures (300 °C) and high pressures (60 atm)
  - Fermentation requires a low, controlled temperature (typically 25–35 °C) because higher temperatures would denature the yeast enzymes acting as the catalyst

parts.problemMd:
A student carries out a titration to determine the concentration of a dilute acid using a standard alkali.

Five actions in this acid-base titration are shown in the table.

| step | action |
|---|---|
| P | record the final burette reading after the end-point is reached |
| Q | transfer a measured volume of alkali into a conical flask using a volumetric pipette |
| R | add a few drops of a suitable indicator to the flask |
| S | note the initial burette reading before starting the titration |
| T | carefully run the acid from the burette into the flask while swirling until a permanent colour change occurs |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

To answer this question correctly, you must apply your practical knowledge of the standard experimental sequence for an acid-base titration

- **Step 1 (Action Q):** First, a volumetric pipette is used to accurately measure a fixed volume of the standard alkali and transfer it into the conical flask
- **Step 2 (Action R):** Next, a few drops of a suitable indicator are added to the alkali in the flask so the end-point can be visualised
- **Step 3 (Action S):** Before opening the burette tap, the initial volume of the acid in the burette must be read and recorded
- **Step 4 (Action T):** The acid is carefully run from the burette into the flask while swirling, stopping exactly when the indicator permanently changes colour
- **Step 5 (Action P):** Finally, the final volume of the acid in the burette is recorded so the total titre can be calculated

The correct sequence is therefore **Q → R → S → T → P**

**B **&** C **are incorrect because the indicator was added after opening the burette tap. The indicator must be added  before opening the tap because otherwise there is no colour change, and the end point will not be seen

**D **is incorrect because it suggests adding the acid to reach the end-point before noting the initial burette reading . If the starting volume is not recorded before the acid is released, it is impossible to calculate how much acid was actually used!

choices.label: A

A student reacts aqueous silver nitrate with aqueous sodium chloride. A white precipitate of silver chloride is formed in a solution of sodium nitrate. The reaction mixture is filtered to separate the precipitate.

| **A** | silver chloride | aqueous sodium nitrate |
| **B** | aqueous sodium nitrate | silver chloride |
| **C** | silver chloride | pure water |
| **D** | silver nitrate | aqueous sodium chloride |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Silver nitrate reacts with sodium chloride to form silver chloride, which is insoluble and appears as a white precipitate
- Insoluble solids are trapped on the filter paper during filtration and form the residue
- The remaining liquid that passes through the filter paper is the filtrate
- Aqueous sodium nitrate is a soluble side product from the mixture
- The filtrate contains aqueous sodium nitrate, which stays dissolved in water
- Therefore, the **residue is silver chloride and filtrate is aqueous sodium nitrate**

**B **is incorrect because aqueous sodium nitrate is soluble and cannot be the residue, because it will go through the filter paper

**C **is incorrect because the filtrate is not pure water because sodium nitrate is dissolved in it. **The filtration process does not remove the soluble salt from the mixture**

parts.problemMd:
The *R*<sub>f</sub> values of three different pigments are shown in the table.

| pigment | *R*<sub>f</sub> value |
|---|---|
| P | 0.43 |
| Q | 0.57 |
| R | 0.75 |

A student carries out chromatography on an unknown sample. The resulting chromatogram is shown below

![Chromatogram. Baseline at 0.0 cm. Solvent front at 7.0 cm. One sample spot at 3.0 cm above baseline. Ruler shown 0.0–7.0 cm.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/12-experimental-techniques-and-chemical-analysis/12-2-separation-and-purification/assets/001-chromatogram-baseline-at-0-0-cm-solvent-front-at.png)

What is the identity of the unknown pigment?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- To identify the pigment, you must calculate the *R*<sub>f</sub> value of the unknown spot using the formula:

$R_{f}=\frac{\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{substance}}{\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{solvent}}$

- Using the diagram:

![Chromatogram. Horizontal baseline at 0.0 cm. Horizontal solvent front line at 7.0 cm. One spot at 3.0 cm above baseline. Vertical arrows show 3.0 cm (spot) and 7.0 cm (solvent front).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/12-experimental-techniques-and-chemical-analysis/12-2-separation-and-purification/assets/002-chromatogram-horizontal-baseline-at-0-0-cm-horiz.png)

- Distance travelled by substance = 3.0 cm
- Distance travelled by solvent (solvent front) = 7.0 cm

$R_{f}=\frac{3.0}{7.0}=0.428..=0.43$

- Comparing this to the table, the unknown sample matches **pigment P **

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always measure the distance from the **baseline to the centre of the spot**, not the top or bottom. Using the centre of the spot ensures accurate **Rf values** and avoids losing marks for measurement errors.

- On the addition of acidified silver nitrate, iodide ions produce a yellow precipitate:

  - Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + I<sup>–</sup> (aq) → AgI (s)
- The flame test results indicate the substance contains the potassium ion, K<sup>+</sup>
- Hence, the unknown substance is potassium iodide

**A** and **B** are incorrect as lithium ions produce a red-coloured flame

**D** is incorrect as bromide ions produce a cream-coloured precipitate with acidified silver nitrate

parts.problemMd:
Metal cations can be detected using flame tests.

Which row correctly describes the colour of the flame for each metal cation?

| ** ** | **Li**<sup>**+**</sup> | **Ba**<sup>**2+**</sup> | **Ca**<sup>**2+**</sup> |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | lilac | green | yellow |
| **B** | red | green | orange |
| **C** | green | orange | red |
| **D** | red | blue | orange |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- The lithium ion, Li<sup>+</sup>, produces a red flame
- The barium ion, Ba<sup>2+</sup>, produces an apple-green flame
- The calcium ion, Ca<sup>2+</sup>, produces an orange-red flame

**A** is incorrect as lilac is the colour for potassium ions and yellow is the colour for sodium ions

**C** is incorrect as the colours are correct but they are not matched to the appropriate metal cation

**D** is incorrect as blue is not the colour associated with barium ions

parts.problemMd:
A student tested copper sulfate solution and potassium iodide solution using flame tests using the method shown.

1. Dip a metal wire loop in copper sulfate solution.
2. Put the metal wire loop in a Bunsen burner flame.
3. Record the flame colour produced.
4. Repeat steps 1 to 3 but using potassium iodide solution.

The student’s method did not produce the distinct lilac flame colour using potassium iodide solution.

Which statement would **not** cause the lack of lilac flame?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- The student's method is missing two key points:

  - In step 2, the Bunsen burner flame should be blue / non-luminous so that it does not affect the results
  - Step 4 should talk about cleaning the metal wire loop between testing the copper sulfate solution and potassium iodide solution
  
    - This is done by dipping the metal wire loop into concentrated acid and then placing it into the blue / non-luminous flame
- Option **D** is the only option that ensures the metal wire loop is not contaminated **AND** does not introduce another colour into the flame

**A** is incorrect as overheating the wire loop can cause an orange / red colour in the flame which will mask the pale lilac colour of the potassium ions

**B** is incorrect as the safety flame is an orange / yellow colour which will mask the pale lilac colour of the potassium ions

**C** is incorrect as using the same metal wire loop without cleaning it between tests means that it may be contaminated with copper sulfate from the first flame test

parts.problemMd:
Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Hydrogen gas is produced at the cathode and oxygen gas is produced at the anode.

Which row shows the correct tests for these gases?

|   | test for hydrogen | test for oxygen |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | turns limewater milky | bleaches damp litmus paper |
| **B** | relights a glowing splint | 'pops' with a lighted splint |
| **C** | 'pops' with a lighted splint | relights a glowing splint |
| **D** | 'pops' with a lighted splint | bleaches damp litmus paper |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Hydrogen gas is identified using a lighted splint, which produces a squeaky pop
- Oxygen gas is identified using a glowing splint, which relights in oxygen
- These are the standard gas tests required at IGCSE level

**A **& **D **are incorrect because  bleaching damp litmus paper is a test for chlorine, not oxygen

**B **is incorrect because the gas tests are reversed

| **Test** | **Observation** |
|---|---|
| Acidified silver nitrate added | Cream precipitate formed |
| Aqueous sodium hydroxide added | Red-brown precipitate formed |

What is the solid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B ****because:**

- Bromide ions produce a cream precipitate with acidified silver nitrate as insoluble silver bromide is formed
- Iron(III) ions produce a red-brown precipitate when aqueous sodium hydroxide is added

**A** is incorrect as iron(II) ions produce a green precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide

**C** is incorrect as iron(II) ions produce a green precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide and chloride ions produce a white precipitate with acidified silver nitrate

**D** is incorrect as chloride ions produce a white precipitate with acidified silver nitrate

parts.problemMd: Which reaction would result in the production of a gas that would produce a squeaky pop with a lit splint?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- When magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid, magnesium chloride and hydrogen gas are produced:

  - magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen
- Hydrogen gas will produce a squeaky pop with a lit splint

**A** is incorrect as when iron(II) oxide and sulfuric acid react, iron(II) sulfate and water are produced in a neutralisation reaction. No gas is produced

**B** is incorrect as when methane and oxygen react during complete combustion, carbon dioxide and water are produced. No hydrogen is produced

**D** is incorrect as during photosynthesis, carbon dioxide and water react in the presence of light and chlorophyll to form oxygen and glucose. No hydrogen gas is produced

parts.problemMd: Which statement about aqueous sodium hydroxide is correct?

- When sodium hydroxide reacts with aluminium ions, it forms a white precipitate
- The precipitate will dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide to form a colourless solution

**A** is incorrect as when added to a solution containing nitrate ions and aluminium foil and then warmed, ammonia will be given off which will turn moist red litmus paper blue

parts.problemMd:
The results of different chemical tests on a solution of compound **Y **are shown.

| **Test** | **Result** |
|---|---|
| Acidified barium nitrate added | White precipitate formed |
| Aqueous sodium hydroxide added | White precipitate formed, soluble in excess |
| Aqueous ammonia added | White precipitate formed, insoluble in excess |

What is compound **Y**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- Aluminium ions form a white precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide that is soluble in excess
- Aluminium ions form a white precipitate with aqueous ammonia that is insoluble in excess
- Sulfate ions form a white precipitate of barium sulfate when acidified barium nitrate is added

**B** is incorrect as chloride ions don't form a white precipitate with barium nitrate as barium chloride is soluble

**C** is incorrect as the white precipitate formed when aqueous ammonia is added to a solution containing zinc ions will dissolve in excess

**D** is incorrect as chloride ions don't form a white precipitate with barium nitrate as barium chloride is soluble. The white precipitate formed when aqueous ammonia is added to a solution containing zinc ions will dissolve in exces*s*

parts.problemMd:
A solution of an unknown salt is tested by adding aqueous sodium hydroxide. A blue precipitate is formed which is insoluble in excess.

The mixture is then warmed and aluminium foil is added. A gas is released which turns damp red litmus paper blue.

What is the salt?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- On the addition of aqueous NaOH, copper ions produce a blue-coloured gelatinous precipitate of copper hydroxide which is insoluble in excess
- The litmus paper test indicates that the gas given off is basic
- This indicates that the nitrate ion, NO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup>, is present as ammonia gas is liberated on warming with the addition of NaOH

**B** and **D** are incorrect as the anion determined to be present is the nitrate ion

**C** is incorrect as  the addition of NaOH to an ammonium salt produces sodium nitrate, a highly soluble white salt which does not produce a precipitate

parts.problemMd:
An aqueous solution of sodium carbonate is divided into two portions.

A flame test is carried out on the first portion. Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to the second portion and the gas produced is tested.

Which row gives the correct flame colour and the correct test for the gas produced?

|   | flame colour | test for the gas |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | lilac | turns limewater milky |
| **B** | yellow | 'pops' with a lighted splint |
| **C** | yellow | turns limewater milky |
| **D** | lilac | 'pops' with a lighted splint |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

To solve this, you must identify the cation and the anion in sodium carbonate, and know their respective chemical tests

- **Flame colour (Sodium ion, Na**<sup>**+**</sup>**): **

  - The syllabus states that a flame test for sodium produces a **yellow** flame
- **Gas produced (Carbonate ion, **CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>**):**

  - When a carbonate reacts with a dilute acid (such as hydrochloric acid), it produces a salt, water, and **carbon dioxide gas**
- **Test for the gas:**

  - The standard test for carbon dioxide is that it **turns limewater milky**. (This eliminates option B, as a lighted splint causing a 'pop' is the test for hydrogen gas)

Therefore, the **flame is yellow and the gas turns limewater milky**

**A** & **D** are incorrect as a lilac flame indicates the presence of potassium

**B** is incorrect as a lighted splint causing a 'pop' is the test for hydrogen gas

parts.problemMd:
A student is given a white insoluble solid to analyse. He first added hydrochloric acid and observed bubbles of colourless gas. He then added a small amount of aqueous ammonia to the solid-acid mixture and observed a white precipitate being formed. The precipitate dissolved in excess aqueous ammonia.

What is the identity of the white solid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The carbonates of zinc are insoluble in water
- All metal carbonates react with acids to produce carbon dioxide / CO<sub>2</sub> gas, salt and water
- The positive zinc ion, Zn<sup>2+</sup>, forms a white precipitate with the addition of ammonia

  - The white precipitate re-dissolves when ammonia is added in excess

**A** and **B** are incorrect as the nitrate salts are soluble

**D** is incorrect as although calcium carbonate is insoluble, it produces only a very small amount of precipitate with the addition of aqueous ammonia

parts.problemMd:
Aqueous sodium hydroxide is used in chemical analysis.

Which statement about aqueous NaOH is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- Iron(II) ions react with aqueous sodium hydroxide to produce a green-coloured precipitate which is iron(II) hydroxide:

  - Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2OH<sup>–</sup> (aq) → Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s)
- Iron(II) is insoluble in excess NaOH

**A** is incorrect as sodium sulfate is produced which is highly soluble, hence a precipitate is not formed

**C **is incorrect as the iron(II) hydroxide produced is insoluble in excess NaOH, hence it does not dissolve

**D** is incorrect as ammonia gas is produced which is basic, not acidic:  NH<sub>4</sub>Cl + NaOH → NaCl + NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

parts.problemMd: A student analysed a solution and found it to contain ions of silver and barium. What could the identity of the anion be?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- The question states that the solution contains both Ba<sup>2+</sup> and Ag<sup>+</sup> ions, so the anion with which they are combined must be water soluble
- Only nitrates of both barium and silver are soluble in water

**B** and **D** are incorrect as  BaSO<sub>4</sub> is insoluble in water as are the carbonates of silver and barium

**C** is incorrect as AgCl is insoluble in water

parts.problemMd:
A student placed a small volume of an unknown solution into two separate test tubes labelled 1 and 2. He added a few drops of aqueous NaOH to each test tube and observed a green precipitate being formed. The precipitate dissolved on the addition of excess sodium hydroxide in test 1 but the precipitate remained in test tube 2.

Which ions must be present in test tubes 1 and 2?

| ** ** | **test tube 1** | **test tube 2** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Ca<sup>2+</sup> | Cu<sup>2+</sup> |
| **B** | Cu<sup>2+</sup> | Ca<sup>2+</sup> |
| **C** | Fe<sup>2+</sup> | Cr<sup>3+</sup> |
| **D** | Cr<sup>3+</sup> | Fe<sup>2+</sup> |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- Cr<sup>3+</sup> ions form a green precipitate of chromium(III) hydroxide on the addition of sodium hydroxide which is soluble in excess alkali:

  - Cr<sup>3+</sup> + 3OH<sup>–</sup> → Cr(OH)<sub>3</sub>
- Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions form a green gelatinous precipitate on the addition of NaOH which is insoluble in excess alkali:

  - Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 2OH<sup>–</sup> → Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub>

**A** and **B** are incorrect as in NaOH, Ca<sup>2+</sup> forms a whiter precipitate and Cu<sup>2+</sup> forms a pale blue precipitate, both of which are insoluble in excess

**C** is incorrect as the ions are placed in the wrong order

parts.problemMd:
A substance produces a gas which decolourises acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) when warmed with dilute HCl. It produces a yellow-coloured flame in the flame test.

What is the substance?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The sulfite ion, SO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup>, when treated with HCl will decolourise acidified potassium manganate(VII)
- The yellow colour flame indicates the presence of the sodium ion, Na<sup>+</sup>

**A** and **D** are incorrect as the results indicate the presence of the sulfite ion, not bromide

**B** is incorrect as potassium ions produce a lilac-coloured flame
